zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical review aid: NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510, CC BY 4.0 (https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Consulted after independent scan reading; the transcription and review notes are this reviewer's work, not a reproduction of the index.

runs.text: ſe deixa em aberto por reuerencia da peßoa a q̃

lines.note: Continues f412's account of a blank portion of a letter, left out of respect for the addressee. A fold obscures part of por; the visible residue and continuous phrase support that reading rather than OCR za. The crop is enlarged to include the sloping right end.
Completes the reference to the person being addressed. Raixiuo voqu begins the example about leaving respectful blank space; its spelling contrasts with printed Ranxi on f412.

runs.text: este papel em aberto, & limpo no principio

lines.note: Translates leaving the paper blank and clean at the beginning. The phrase continues to specify the beginning of the letter; no missing material is invented across the damaged fold.
Completes the explanation of blank space at the beginning of a letter. This finishes the entry carried over from the previous page.
Raixi gives principal forms for venerating or showing reverence. The abbreviated ita is preserved rather than expanded to a full inflected form in the transcription.

runs.text: Vida futura, ou a outra vida.

lines.note: Raixǒ means the future or other life. The real space in outra vida is restored, and the final S. is an upright usage label.
Raixǔ denotes the coming autumn. The final vowel has a caron and the explanatory aqi supplies the season; S. is upright.
Raixun denotes the coming spring. The Japanese verb reads Qitaru, not Qitaiu; primauera is continuous rather than the OCR's internally divided word.
Completes the coming-spring definition. The final S. is a register label following the short Portuguese continuation.
Raiyu is equated with Yurai and glossed as cause or origin. The scan clearly supplies initial R and capital Y, correcting OCR Faiyu and rurai.
Ramǒ is glossed by Japanese ami and Portuguese rede, a net. The caron in the headword remains distinct from the plain vowels of the synonym.
Ran denotes disorder or disturbance. The example begins Ranuo vocoſu, causing a disturbance, with its verb divided across the physical rows.
Completes vocoſu and its translation, then begins the next example with Ran-. Both physical divisions are retained rather than merged into continuous lines.
Completes Ranga deqita, a disturbance arising. The Portuguese begins perturbação at the edge without a secure hyphen, so none is supplied.
Completes warlike disturbance and gives a closely related Japanese example with ideqitaru. The latter form remains distinct from deqita above.
Idem refers back to the previous example; Ranga iqu is another expression for the occurrence of disturbance. The initial is R rather than OCR B, and the Portuguese definition continues below.
Completes disturbance of war. The printed joining deguerra is preserved rather than silently separated.

runs.text: Certo modo de tanger o tabaquinho.

lines.note: Ranbiǒxi denotes a particular way of playing the small drum. The Portuguese noun tabaquinho is one word; the apparent OCR space was introduced by damage.
Ranbǒ concerns disorderly interference, glossed specifically as pillaging or robbery. The next row completes the second Portuguese infinitive and gives an example.
Completes robbing and gives Ranbǒ suru. The repeated headword has n, not the OCR's u; the initial damaged Portuguese letters remain recoverable as roubar.
Ranbu is a performance involving dance and song, with a Japanese paraphrase about dancing. The headword is Ranbu, not OCR Babu; the dance verb's caron is retained.
Completes dance and song, then illustrates performing this entertainment. The visible Portuguese verb is Fazer, not OCR Farzer, and folguedo is divided across the rows.
Completes folguedo and its open-ended qualification. This short row belongs to the Ranbu example.
Rancan and Vobaxima refer to a balustrade or railing, here on a bridge. The historical Balauſtes is retained without adding an expected r.
Adds verandas as another location for the balustrades. It completes the examples of where Rancan occurs.
Randa means neglect or lack of care. The Japanese explanatory phrase is read with that sense; Portuguese negligencia is divided at the edge.
Completes negligencia. The upright S. marks written usage and is not italicized with the final word.
Randat describes disorder in one's life or conduct. The final t is part of the headword and remains visible in its derived example below.
Adds conduct or customs and describes a disorderly person. The scan includes t in Randatna, omitted by OCR Randana; Ho- begins homem.
Completes a person whose life is disorderly. This is the translation of Randatna fito, not a new evaluative headword.
Rango means after the disturbance, as Midareno nochi explicitly states. The initial of Midareno is M, not OCR X; perturbação is divided across the rows.
Completes disturbance or upheaval of war. It specifies the event after which Rango places something.
Rangocu describes a kingdom in disorder, matching Midaruru cuni. The headword has n rather than the OCR's u.
Ranguequi is defined as revolt or disturbance, with Midare as its Japanese explanation. The Portuguese word continues on the next physical row.
Completes perturbação, the second gloss of Ranguequi. This short continuation is not an independent entry.
Ranguicu names a fragrant herb, with Araragui qicu as the Japanese explanation. The scan reads Ranguicu, not OCR Fanguieu, and cheiroſa rather than cheinoſa.

runs.text: chamada. Item, A flor desta erua.

lines.note: Completes the herb definition and adds its flower as a second sense. The short s in desta is retained as printed.
Ranguiǒ concerns improper conduct, explained by Midarini voconǒ. The scan supplies initial M and Portuguese Obras, correcting OCR Xidarini and Gbras.

runs.text: torpes, & deſordenadas, ou peccados de tor-

lines.note: Qualifies the actions as shameful and disorderly and begins the alternative expression peccados de torpeza. The division tor- continues below.
Completes torpeza in the description of improper or shameful acts. This row belongs to the Ranguiǒ definition.

Raiguiocu has ranqiocu as an alternative form; lowercase l introduces an alternative rather than being a numeral. The gloss begins a manner of playing or singing. The first o of modo is damaged and c-like; modo is the chosen contextual reading, not a silent claim that the glyph is clear.

runs.text: ger, ou cantar picado, ou apreßado de quando

lines.note: Completes tanger and describes a pointed or hurried manner of singing at intervals. The printed ending is ger, not get, and the beta-like double-s sort in apreßado is retained.
Completes de quando em quando, specifying intermittent changes in the musical performance. It belongs to Raiguiocu rather than the next entry.
Ranguiǒjin denotes a person of improper conduct. The scan has the beta-like double-s sort in Peßoa and reads deſhonesta, not the garbled OCR deſhorefta; the local st ligature is rendered st.
Ranguiǒna expresses the same description adjectivally, illustrated by Ranguiǒna fito. Both occurrences retain the caron over o.

runs.text: Estacada que ſe faz nalgum caminho,

lines.note: Ranguy denotes a stockade or line of stakes across a route. The initial is R rather than OCR B, and the definition continues through the column break.

runs.text: ou paſsagem muito ao comprido pẽra não deixar

lines.note: Describes the long barrier across a passage, intended to prevent entry. The words are muito, não, and deixar, not the OCR's maido, nã, and deinar; the locally visible mixed paſsagem is retained.
Completes the purpose of excluding enemies and begins the example Ranguyuo vtçu, setting up the stakes. This is the continuation from the foot of the first column.
Translates Ranguyuo vtçu as fixing the timbers or stakes in place. The two local st spellings are retained rather than globally harmonized.
Ran-in denotes disorder in matters of lust. The internal hyphen belongs to the printed headword, not to a physical line break.
Ranja denotes something fragrant. Mini ranjauo begins an example about applying fragrance to oneself and continues with its verb below.

runs.text: Por cheiro, ou defumarſe de ma-

lines.note: Completes the example's verb and translates applying scent or perfuming oneself with smoke. The f of defumarſe is lexical, unlike the long s later in the same word.
Completes maneira and explains the resulting fragrance on the person. The abbreviation tilde in cheirãdo is preserved rather than expanded.

runs.text: Certa eſpecie de calambà muito fina,

lines.note: Ranjatai is described as a very fine kind of fragrant calambà. The grave over the final a is retained; the gloss continues with the object's reported origin and place of keeping.

runs.text: que antiguamente veo da China, & ainda oje

lines.note: The dictionary says that it came from China long ago and remained preserved at the time of writing. Antiguamente is printed as one word, correcting the OCR split.
Completes the reported place of preservation, Nara. Nara is a Japanese place name embedded inside a Portuguese explanation and is retained in the locally printed italic text.
Ranman describes luxuriant flowering, with Midare fabicoru as its Japanese explanation. The Portuguese begins a definition continued over the next two rows.

runs.text: roſas, ou flores quando eſtão muitas hũas ſobre

lines.note: Specifies roses or flowers growing densely one over another. The tildes in eſtão and hũas are kept on their printed vowels.
Completes the image of overlapping flowers. S. is an upright written-usage label rather than part of the italic Portuguese sentence.
This Ranmǒ means improper desires, as Midarinaru nozomi indicates. Its V-shaped caron is visibly distinct from the tilde in the following clothing-pattern entry Ranmõ.
Completes bad or disorderly desires. The final S. is upright and marks written usage.

runs.text: Lauores, ou pinturas de veſtidos que

lines.note: Ranmõ concerns decorative work or patterns on clothing. The second pass and enlarged crop show a tilde, not the V-shaped caron of the preceding Ranmǒ; the two entries must not be conflated. The local supplied ſt spelling in veſtidos is retained.
Describes patterns distributed without an orderly arrangement. It qualifies the clothing decoration, not the desires in the preceding entry.

Rannhǔ describes an unruly crowd entering, matching Midare iru rather than OCR Xidare. The second pass restores the visible comma after romania. Its medial letter looks like n, so romania is retained instead of silently substituting expected romaria; that consonant remains a nonblocking reading caveat.
Completes the description of many people entering in a disorderly rush. The final S. is upright.
Rannicu concerns deteriorating flesh or meat, explained by Tadareta xiximura. The following rows describe its spoiled appearance.

runs.text: moſtra danarſe, ou corromperſe por estar ara-

lines.note: Describes meat showing damage or corruption. Enlargement gives ara- rather than OCR ama- at the edge; the resulting araganhada is preserved without substituting a more familiar Portuguese form.
Completes the description of damaged or shrivelled flesh, including the printed expression com beiços. The historical wording is retained, and the closing S. is upright.
Ranpat means disordered hair, here described as loose. The checked final t is part of the Japanese headword and is not expanded.
Adds tangled or entangled hair. The printed cedilla in empeçados is retained, and S. is a separate upright usage label.
Ranpǒ describes a troubled kingdom, as Midareta cuni states. Its caron contrasts with the circumflex of the following bird name.

Ranpô is connected with Ranqei and fôuǒ and defined as a large bird. The circumflex in Ranpô must not be assimilated to the preceding Ranpǒ. The very short edge mark after grã is retained as the supplied division mark.

runs.text: de, & fermoſo que ha na China, & outro da

lines.note: Completes grande and describes a beautiful bird reported in China, then begins comparison with another of the same kind. This remains the dictionary's description rather than a modern zoological identification.

runs.text: meſma laya que chamamos paßaro do ſol.

lines.note: Completes the comparison with what the dictionary calls the bird of the sun. The historical term and double-s sort are preserved.
Ranqei points back to Ranpô. The cross-reference begins with R, not OCR B, and retains the circumflex distinguishing the bird entry.
Ran and qei here denote two kinds of fragrant herbs, distinct from the bird cross-reference above. The comma and intervening space are visibly printed.

This complete physical row was omitted by OCR and is restored between c2-l029 and c2-l030 without renumbering later IDs. Ranqiacu is explained with Midare, ruru and a Portuguese gloss of disturbance or revolt; the existing reuolta row completes this entry, not the herb entry above.
Completes the restored Ranqiacu definition as disturbance or revolt. The upright S. marks written usage; the row is correctly associated with the newly restored line above.
Ranqiocu points to Raiguiocu, the musical-performance term in the first column. This cross-reference confirms the relationship without changing the printed spelling of either form.
Ransǒ denotes densely growing, tangled plants, explained by Midaretaru cuſa. The short s in the headword and long s in cuſa are separate local forms, both preserved.
Completes the description of plants intertwined with each other. Hũas retains its abbreviation mark, and the usage label is upright.

This Ransǒ is the name of a fragrant herb, explained as Araraguino cuſa, rather than the tangled vegetation of the preceding entry. Its short s remains distinct from the long s in the following Ranſo.
Completes the statement that the herb is so called. It is the short Portuguese continuation of the second Ransǒ entry.
Ranſo concerns making accusations improperly, as Midarini vttayuru indicates. The long s in the headword and the grave in mà are retained.
Completes the description of an improper or disorderly accusation and begins the example Ranſo ſuru. The verb follows on the next row.
Completes the Japanese example with ſuru. Both the verb and the closing S. are upright; the label should not be italicized as Portuguese prose.
Rantǒ is described as an arrangement of square and round stones. The scan reads redondas, not OCR redendas, and the definition continues below.

runs.text: hũas ſobre outras como tumulo que poem os gen-

lines.note: Describes stones placed one on another as a tomb monument. The noun is tumulo with m rather than OCR tunulo, and gen- continues into the next row.
Completes gentios and the description of monuments placed over graves. The religious designation belongs to the historical Portuguese source, not to the reviewer's terminology.
Ran-vn denotes scattered clouds, matching Midaregumo. The hyphen is internal to the headword, whereas its use in the next example is written with a space.
Illustrates clouds drifting in the sky. Ran vn is visibly separated without a hyphen, tadayô has a circumflex, and the Portuguese verb is divided an-/dão.
Completes the description of scattered clouds moving in the air. The final S. is upright and belongs to the written example.
Ranxei means a world in disorder, as Midareta yo indicates. The initial is R, correcting OCR Banxei.

runs.text: ou cheo de reuoltas de guerra.

lines.note: Completes a world full of upheavals of war. This is the final body row, separate from the signature and catchword beneath it.
